Why is Countess Mary worried about little Nicholas?

"Ah, Nicholas, do you know I am often troubled about little Nicholas," said Countess Mary. "He is such an exceptional boy. I am afraid I neglect him in favor of my own: we all have children and relations while he has no one. He is constantly alone with his thoughts."
She fears she neglects him in favour of her own children. Unlike them, he has no parents or close family and is often alone with his thoughts.

By the wilderness of casks that I had walked on long ago, and on which the rain of years had fallen since, rotting them in many places, and leaving miniature swamps and pools of water upon those that stood on end, I made my way to the ruined garden. I went all round it; round by the corner where Herbert and I had fought our battle; round by the paths where Estella and I had walked. So cold, so lonely, so dreary all!

What does Pip see as he walks through the old brewery and garden?

He finds rotting casks with small pools of water on them and a ruined garden. He goes round the corner where he fought Herbert and the paths where he walked with Estella, and finds it all cold, lonely and dreary.

What news interrupts the conversation, and what do the women say?

Whilst we were talking one came running and breathlessly gasped out that the body of Skinsky had been found inside the wall of the churchyard of St. Peter, and that the throat had been torn open as if by some wild animal. Those we had been speaking with ran off to see the horror, the women crying out "This is the work of a Slovak!" We hurried away lest we should have been in some way drawn into the affair, and so detained.

Someone runs up out of breath to say that Skinsky's body has been found inside the churchyard wall of St. Peter, with the throat torn open as if by a wild animal. The women cry out that it is the work of a Slovak.

Why is pitchpoling with a harpoon rare?

But before going further, it is important to mention here, that though the harpoon may be pitchpoled in the same way with the lance, yet it is seldom done; and when done, is still less frequently successful, on account of the greater weight and inferior length of the harpoon as compared with the lance, which in effect become serious drawbacks. As a general thing, therefore, you must first get fast to a whale, before any pitchpoling comes into play.
The harpoon is heavier and shorter than the lance, which makes it less successful. So the boat must first get fast to a whale before pitchpoling comes into play.

This is from a book I am reading.

Tashtego stood in the bows. He was full of the fire of the hunt. He hated Pip for a poltroon. Snatching the boat-knife from its sheath, he suspended its sharp edge over the line, and turning towards Stubb, exclaimed interrogatively, "Cut?" Meantime Pip's blue, choked face plainly looked, Do, for God's sake! All passed in a flash. In less than half a minute, this entire thing happened.

What does Tashtego do with the boat-knife?
He snatches it from its sheath and holds its sharp edge over the line. He turns to Stubb and asks "Cut?", while Pip's blue, choked face seems to plead "Do, for God's sake!"

I am reading this book and have a question.

These words cut me: yet what could I do or I say? I ought probably to have done or said nothing; but I was so tortured by a sense of remorse at thus hurting his feelings, I could not control the wish to drop balm where I had wounded.

Why does the speaker want to say something kind after the words that cut?
The speaker is tortured by remorse for hurting his feelings and cannot resist the urge to soothe the hurt they caused.

"The Gandharva continued, 'This, O Partha, is the history of Tapati of old, the daughter of Vivaswat. It is for her that thou art (called) Tapatya. King Samvarana begot upon Tapati a son named Kuru, who was the foremost of ascetics. Born in the race of Kuru, thou art, O Arjuna, to be called Tapatya.'"

Why is Arjuna called Tapatya?
King Samvarana had a son named Kuru by Tapati, the daughter of Vivaswat. Arjuna, born in the race of Kuru, is therefore called Tapatya, after Tapati.

Rostov, smoking his pipe and turning his head about as the water trickled down his neck, listened inattentively, with an occasional glance at Ilyin, who was pressing close to him. This officer, a lad of sixteen who had recently joined the regiment, was now in the same relation to Nicholas that Nicholas had been to Denisov seven years before. Ilyin tried to imitate Rostov in everything and adored him as a girl might have done.

Answer from the text. How is Ilyin connected to Rostov, and how does Ilyin behave toward Rostov?
Ilyin is a lad of sixteen who recently joined the regiment, and stands to Nicholas Rostov as Nicholas once stood to Denisov. Ilyin tries to imitate Rostov in everything and adores him.

When Pablo came out of the school gate at three o'clock, he could not find his father's car at the usual place. He looked up and down the road and saw only strangers. His chest felt tight, and he held his bag straps with both hands. Then he remembered what his teacher had told them: if you are ever lost, go back to a safe adult. He walked slowly back inside, found the security guard at the gate, and told him his name and class. A few minutes later, his father rushed in, out of breath, saying his car had a flat tyre.

How did Pablo feel when he could not find the car?
He felt scared and worried. The passage says his chest felt tight and he held his bag straps with both hands.

When the storm knocked out the lights in the Baker house, six-year-old Poppy sat in the corner of the sofa gripping a cushion. Each flash of lightning made her jump. Her older brother Sam saw her face and went to find a torch. He turned it on beneath his chin and told her a ghost story, but with a silly twist: the ghost was afraid of thunder too. Poppy giggled, then laughed. By the time the next flash came, she was holding the torch herself, pointing it at the ceiling to make shadows. The storm kept going, but she did not notice.

Why did Poppy stop noticing the storm?
Sam's silly story and the torch games took her mind off her fear.

Our family tried three times to keep a pet bird, but each one flew away when the cage was open. After the third, my mother said no more birds. My brother Vikram quietly began to leave a dish of seeds on the window ledge. Each morning, small sparrows came to eat. He counted them and drew them in a notebook, giving each a name. By the end of the month, twelve sparrows came every day, and one even perched on the window frame while he sat nearby. Our mother watched this from the kitchen and never said a word about the dish.

What does the mother's silence about the dish suggest?
It suggests she accepted the dish and was quietly pleased, because she watched the sparrows from the kitchen and never told him to stop.

Mrs. Banerjee had put out her best cups for the guests from the city. They arrived with a car full of gifts, and spent the evening admiring the hand-woven curtains and the polished brass lamp. When Mrs. Banerjee mentioned that she had made the curtains herself, one guest said, without looking, that they were very nice for a village house. Mrs. Banerjee's smile stayed, but the teapot she was holding trembled slightly. After the guests left, she took down the curtains and folded them into the chest. Her daughter watched in silence and knew the curtains would not go up again.

Why did Mrs. Banerjee take down the curtains?
The guest's remark hurt her pride, so she no longer wanted to display them.

Ants have been marching along the kitchen wall of Pooja's house for two days. They come in a neat brown line from a crack near the window and go straight to the sugar jar. Her mother tried wiping the wall twice, but the line came back each time. Then Pooja remembered that their science teacher had said ants leave a scent trail for others to follow. She took a wet cloth with a little vinegar and scrubbed the whole path from the crack to the shelf. The next morning, the ants were wandering about the wall in confusion, and there was no line at all.

Why did the ants wander in confusion the next morning?
Pooja cleaned away their scent trail with vinegar, so they could no longer follow it.

At her friend's wedding in Udaipur, Sonal was asked to hold the bride's bouquet during the vows. She was so busy watching that she almost forgot it was in her hand. The groom's father leaned over and whispered that she should keep it steady, because it was going to be thrown at the end. When the moment came, Sonal handed it to the bride, who turned and threw it straight at her. She caught it with both hands, and the crowd cheered. Sonal blushed and hid her face behind the flowers, and her friends teased her all evening.

What did Sonal do after she caught the bouquet?
She blushed and hid her face behind the flowers.

At the school sports festival, little Dhruv was sure he would lose his race. He was the smallest in the group, and his legs were short. The starting whistle blew, and he ran with all his might, but he fell behind. Near the finish line, he saw the others stop and turn around. Dhruv, sweating, kept running. When he finally crossed the line, a loud cheer broke out, and his classmates lifted him on their shoulders. Though he had come last, the crowd treated him like a champion. Dhruv's grin was so wide that his cheeks hurt.

Why did the classmates cheer for Dhruv?
Because he never gave up and kept running to the end even though he was last.

The journey from our village to the district town begins at the bus stop beside the school. Every morning at seven, a blue bus arrives, honking twice. It stops at the market, the post office and the old well before turning onto the highway. The ride takes forty minutes. Most passengers are farmers carrying sacks of onions or women carrying baskets of eggs. The conductor, Mr. Kumar, knows who will be late and holds the bus for them. On the way back, the bus leaves the town at five and often arrives after sunset. Children on the back seat sing film songs to pass the time.

What colour is the bus that comes to the village?
The bus that comes is blue.

At night in the forest near Kaziranga, a researcher named Dr. Bora set up a camera trap beside a muddy path. The next morning, she checked the pictures. There were deer, a wild boar and a small fox. In one picture a rhino stood with her calf only a metre from the lens. Dr. Bora printed that photograph and pinned it on the wall of the field office. Visitors often stopped to look at it. She said that the camera showed her more than days of walking ever did, because the animals did not know they were being watched.

Why did the camera show Dr. Bora more than walking in the forest?
Because the animals did not know they were being watched, so they behaved naturally.

For her science project, Dhara grew two sets of radish seeds, one on a sunny window sill and one in a dark cupboard. After a week, the seedlings in the cupboard were long, thin and almost white. Those on the sill were short, sturdy and green. She noted her results and drew both sets with coloured pencils. Her teacher asked her what she thought the plants needed. Dhara said sunlight, because the dark ones looked sick and stretched upward. The teacher praised her answer and then gave her a larger pot so she could move her healthy plants outdoors.

What clue led Dhara to say that plants need sunlight?
The seedlings in the dark cupboard were long, thin and pale, while those on the sunny sill were short, sturdy and green.

A kind of fruit bat lived in the old fig tree in a Mumbai suburb. At dusk, dozens of them unfolded their wings and flew off to find fruit. One evening, a boy named Nikhil put a small basket of overripe bananas on the wall at the top of the steps, and some of the bats landed for a bite. He filmed them with his father's camera. At school the next day, he showed the film, and everyone gasped. His teacher asked if he had touched the bats, and Nikhil said no, he had stayed very still.

What did Nikhil put out for the bats?
He put out a small basket of overripe bananas.

Katie noticed that the leaves on her family's plants in Dublin curled and dropped when winter came. She asked her father if the plants were dying. He said that some trees drop their leaves to save water and energy when it is cold and there is less sunlight. In spring, new leaves would open. Katie marked the tree in her garden with a bright ribbon and wrote down the date of the first fallen leaf. When April came, she sat under the tree and counted the new buds. She was delighted and told everyone it had come back to life.

Why did the trees drop their leaves in winter?
To save water and energy when it is cold and there is less sunlight.
